chapters.title: Chapter 3: Understanding Your Income and Tax

lessons.title: The Five Heads of Income Explained for First-Time Filers

body.text: Every rupee you earn belongs in exactly one of five buckets. The bucket decides which deductions you get, which tax rate applies and which ITR form you file. Put income in the wrong bucket and everything downstream goes wrong.

markDefs.definition: The five categories into which all income is classified for computing tax: Salaries, Income from house property, Profits and gains of business or profession, Capital gains, and Income from other sources.

children.text: Section 13 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (Section 14 of the Income-tax Act, 1961) sorts all income into five
heads of income

. Each head has its own rules for what counts as income and what can be deducted. You compute income under each head separately, add them up, and only then apply deductions and slab rates. Once you can sort your income correctly, the ITR form almost fills itself.

body.caption: The Five Heads at a Glance

cells: Salary, bonus, allowances, perquisites, pension from a former employer
Rent from a building you own, residential or commercial
Rent from a flat in Thane
Profits and gains of business or profession
Freelancing, consulting, running a shop, F&O and intraday trading
Weekly Nifty options trading on Zerodha
Profit on selling shares, mutual funds, property, gold
Selling Reliance Industries shares at a profit
The residual head: interest, dividends, certain gifts, family pension, winnings

body.title: Meera's Income for FY 2025-26, by Head (₹)

children.text: Meera, a product manager in Mumbai, has four of the five heads in one year. That is completely normal for a working professional with a rented-out flat and a demat account. Let us go through each head.
Head 1: Salaries

The test is the relationship, not the amount. Income is salary only if it comes from an employer to an employee. That covers basic pay, DA, HRA and other allowances, bonuses, perquisites like a company car, leave encashment while in service, and pension paid by a former employer. From this, Section 19 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (Section 16 of the 1961 Act) allows a standard deduction of ₹75,000 in the new regime or ₹50,000 in the old regime, and in the old regime also professional tax.

columns.label: As an Employee (Salaries)
points: Paid through payroll with a salary slip
Standard deduction of ₹75,000 in the new regime
No deduction for your actual work expenses

columns.label: As a Consultant (Business or Profession)
points: Client deducts TDS on professional fees
Deduct actual expenses like laptop, internet and travel
Or declare 50% of receipts as income under the presumptive scheme

children.text: Head 2: Income from House Property

markDefs.definition: For a let-out property, broadly the rent receivable for the year, less municipal taxes actually paid by the owner. The flat 30% deduction is calculated on this figure.

children.text: This head taxes rent from a building you own, whether it is a flat, a house or a shop. Start with the rent, subtract municipal taxes you paid, and you have the
net annual value

. From that, you get a flat 30% deduction for repairs and upkeep, whatever you actually spent, plus interest on any home loan taken for the property. For a house you live in yourself, the annual value is nil for up to two such properties.

body.caption: Kunal's Let-Out Flat in Thane, FY 2025-26

cells: Less: municipal taxes paid to TMC
Less: standard deduction at 30% of net annual value
Less: interest on home loan for this flat

body.title: Compute the Rental Income
body.prompt: Latha owns a shop in Coimbatore that she rents to a pharmacy for ₹40,000 a month. In FY 2025-26 she paid ₹20,000 in property tax to the municipal corporation. The shop has no loan. What is her income from house property?
body.explanation: Annual rent is ₹40,000 × 12 = ₹4,80,000. Less ₹20,000 property tax gives a net annual value of ₹4,60,000. The 30% standard deduction is ₹1,38,000. With no loan interest, income from house property is ₹4,60,000 − ₹1,38,000 = ₹3,22,000. A commercial shop is still a building, so rent from it falls under house property, not business.

body.text: The 30% deduction is automatic. Kunal gets ₹86,400 whether he spent ₹5,000 or ₹1,00,000 on repairs, and he cannot claim actual repair bills on top of it. One nuance: this head covers buildings and land attached to them. Rent from a bare plot of land with no building on it goes under income from other sources instead.

children.text: Head 3: Profits and Gains of Business or Profession

markDefs.definition: A simplified scheme where a small business or professional declares income at a fixed percentage of turnover or receipts instead of keeping detailed books of accounts.

children.text: Any income from running a business or practising a profession lands here: a freelance designer, a chartered accountant, a tuition centre, a kirana store, a YouTube channel earning ad revenue. So does trading. Futures and options trading is treated as non-speculative business income, and intraday equity trading, where no delivery is taken, is speculative business income. You pay tax on profit after deducting business expenses. Small businesses and professionals can instead opt for a
presumptive taxation
scheme under Section 58 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (Sections 44AD and 44ADA of the 1961 Act).

body.caption: Presumptive Schemes at a Glance, FY 2025-26

cells: Doctors, lawyers, architects, designers, consultants, engineers
Up to ₹75 lakh if cash receipts are within 5%, otherwise ₹50 lakh
Up to ₹3 crore if cash receipts are within 5%, otherwise ₹2 crore
At least 6% of digital receipts and 8% of cash receipts

body.title: Classify the Trader
body.question: Ritika, a software tester in Hyderabad, trades Bank Nifty and Nifty weekly options on Zerodha alongside her job. Under which head does her options trading profit or loss fall?
options: Profits and gains of business or profession
body.explanation: F&O trading is treated as non-speculative business income, even for someone with a full-time job. It is not a capital gain, even though the trades happen on the same app she uses to buy shares. This moves her to ITR-3, and losses can be carried forward for 8 years if she files on time.

children.text: Head 4: Capital Gains

When you sell a capital asset such as shares, mutual fund units, property, gold or bonds, the profit is a capital gain. Whether it is short-term or long-term depends on how long you held the asset. For listed shares and equity mutual funds the dividing line is 12 months. For most other assets, such as property, gold and unlisted shares, it is 24 months. The two types are taxed very differently.

cells: Listed shares and equity mutual funds (STT paid)
12.5% on gains above ₹1.25 lakh under Section 198 (Section 112A of 1961 Act)
Debt mutual funds bought on or after 1 April 2023
Slab rates, always treated as short-term

body.text: A long-term gain of ₹90,000 on equity mutual funds is tax-free because it is within the ₹1.25 lakh exemption, but it must still be reported in your ITR. Leaving it out because the tax is nil is a mismatch waiting to happen, since the sale already shows up in your AIS.

children.text: Head 5: Income from Other Sources

This is the residual head: income that is taxable but does not fit any of the other four. The common items are interest on FDs, RDs, savings accounts and bonds, dividends, family pension received after the death of an employee, interest on an income tax refund, and winnings from lotteries, game shows and online games, which are taxed at a flat 30%. Family pension gets a deduction of one-third of the amount, capped at ₹25,000 in the new regime and ₹15,000 in the old regime.

Gifts need special care. Under Section 92(2)(m) of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (Section 56(2)(x) of the 1961 Act), money or property received without consideration from people who are not relatives is taxable if the total in a year exceeds ₹50,000. Gifts from relatives such as parents, siblings and a spouse, and gifts received on your marriage, are exempt, whatever the amount.

body.label: The Gift Threshold Trap
body.value: Cross ₹50,000 and the whole amount is taxable
body.context: If friends gift you ₹60,000 in total during the year, all ₹60,000 is taxable, not just the ₹10,000 above the limit.

body.title: Lock In the Gift Rule
body.textWithBlank: Gifts of money from non-relatives become taxable when the total received in a year exceeds ₹___.
body.explanation: The threshold is ₹50,000 in aggregate for the year. Once crossed, the entire amount is taxed under income from other sources. Gifts from relatives and gifts received on marriage are fully exempt.

children.text: Sorting Drill: Which Head?
Say your answer out loud before you flip each card. These are the items first-time filers most often put in the wrong place.

cards.term: Pension from your former employer, received after retirement
cards.definition: Salaries. It comes from an employer-employee relationship, so the standard deduction applies.

cards.term: Family pension received after a spouse's death
cards.definition: Income from other sources, with a deduction of one-third, capped at ₹25,000 in the new regime.

cards.term: Rent from letting out a vacant plot of land
cards.definition: Income from other sources. House property covers buildings and land attached to them, not bare land.
Business income, specifically speculative business, because no delivery was taken.

cards.term: Interest received on your income tax refund
cards.definition: Income from other sources, taxable in the year you receive it.

cards.term: Selling a gold coin bought three years ago
cards.definition: Capital gains, long-term, since gold held for more than 24 months is a long-term asset.

cards.term: AdSense revenue from your YouTube cooking channel
cards.definition: Profits and gains of business or profession, with eligible expenses deductible.
Income from other sources, taxed at your slab rate.

body.title: Sort Vivek's Year
body.scenario: Vivek, 31, lives in Pune. In FY 2025-26 he had: salary of ₹16,00,000 from Persistent Systems; rent of ₹2,40,000 from a flat he owns in Nashik; a short-term gain of ₹35,000 on shares held for five months; a long-term gain of ₹90,000 on an equity mutual fund; FD interest of ₹30,000 from HDFC Bank; dividends of ₹8,000; ₹60,000 in cash gifts from college friends at his housewarming; and ₹1,20,000 AdSense income from his tech review YouTube channel.
body.prompt: Place each item under its head, point out any trap, and say what his filing will look like.
body.modelAnswer: Salaries: ₹16,00,000 from Persistent, less the standard deduction. House property: the Nashik rent of ₹2,40,000, less municipal taxes, the 30% deduction and any loan interest. Business or profession: the ₹1,20,000 YouTube income, less eligible expenses such as equipment and internet. Capital gains: the ₹35,000 short-term gain on shares, taxed at 20%, and the ₹90,000 long-term equity mutual fund gain, which is within the ₹1.25 lakh exemption, so the tax is nil but it must still be reported. Other sources: FD interest of ₹30,000, dividends of ₹8,000, and the ₹60,000 of gifts. The trap is the gifts: friends are not relatives and a housewarming is not a marriage, so because the total crossed ₹50,000, the whole ₹60,000 is taxable, not just ₹10,000. Since he has business income from YouTube as well as capital gains, he cannot use ITR-1 or ITR-2. He will most likely file ITR-3, which Chapter 4 explains.

body.title: What about income that is exempt?

children.text: Some receipts fall outside taxable income altogether: PPF interest and maturity, agricultural income, gifts from relatives, and gifts received on marriage, among others. They do not belong to any taxable head, but most ITR forms still ask you to disclose them in the exempt income section. Reporting them keeps your return consistent with your bank credits and AIS, and documents the source of money you may spend or invest later.

body.title: Sort Your Own FY 2025-26 Income
steps: Salaries: list each employer and the gross salary from each Form 16
House property: list each property you own, whether let out or self-occupied, with rent and municipal taxes
Business or profession: note any freelance, consulting, YouTube, F&O or intraday income
Capital gains: pull your broker's tax P&L and mutual fund capital gains statement
Other sources: add up interest, dividends, family pension and any gifts from non-relatives
Exempt income: note PPF interest, agricultural income and gifts from relatives
Count your heads. Business income or capital gains are the two signals that you may need a form other than ITR-1

points: Section 13 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (Section 14 of the 1961 Act) classifies all income into five heads: salaries, house property, business or profession, capital gains and other sources
Salary requires an employer-employee relationship; the same work billed as a consultant is business or profession income
House property income is rent less municipal taxes, a flat 30% deduction and home loan interest; rent from a bare plot goes to other sources
F&O trading is non-speculative business income and intraday equity trading is speculative business income, not capital gains
Listed equity is short-term within 12 months, taxed at 20% under Section 196, with long-term gains above ₹1.25 lakh taxed at 12.5% under Section 198
Other sources is the residual head for interest, dividends, family pension and winnings, and gifts from non-relatives above ₹50,000 in a year are taxable in full

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and does not constitute tax advice. Classification of income can depend on specific facts, and rates, limits and section numbers reflect the position for FY 2025-26 and the Income-tax Act, 2025 at the time of writing. Verify with the Income Tax Department's portal or a qualified tax professional for your situation.
